What the original study did not say

Rosenhan: being sane in insane places

Eight healthy people faked hearing voices and were admitted to psychiatric hospitals. Half a century later, the study is in doubt.

In 1973, Science published David Rosenhan's study. He and seven other healthy volunteers went to psychiatric hospitals saying they heard a voice saying "empty", "hollow" and "thud". All were admitted. Once inside they behaved normally, yet they stayed an average of 19 days and almost all were discharged with a diagnosis of schizophrenia "in remission".

A huge impact

The paper fuelled criticism of psychiatry, contributed to the closure of large hospitals and helped make diagnostic manuals more precise with the DSM-III in 1980.

In 2019, the journalist Susannah Cahalan examined Rosenhan's files and found serious inconsistencies: she could not identify most of the participants, Rosenhan's own medical record described symptoms he did not mention in the paper, and at least one participant whose data did not fit was left out. Today it is seen as a highly questionable study, although the questions it raised about diagnosis remain legitimate.

References

  1. Rosenhan, D. L. (1973). On being sane in insane places. Science, 179(4070), 250–258.
  2. Cahalan, S. (2019). The Great Pretender. Grand Central.
